machu-picchu.story: Imagine arriving at Machu Picchu, a 15th-century Inca citadel in the Eastern Cordillera of southern Peru, set on a mountain ridge at 2,430 meters above the Sacred Valley and along the Urubamba River, where a deep canyon creates a subtropical mountain climate. Often called the “Lost City of the Incas,” it is a major archaeological site and an iconic symbol of the Inca civilization, with finely crafted dry-stone walls and structures including the Temple of the Sun, the Temple of the Three Windows, and the Intihuatana ritual stone. It is believed to have served as an estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti, was abandoned roughly a century later, likely during the Spanish conquest, and was brought to international attention in 1911 by Hiram Bingham III. As you visit this National Historic Sanctuary, UNESCO World Heritage Site, and one of the New Seven Wonders of the World, you join the site’s over 1.5 million annual visitors as of 2025, making it Peru’s most visited international tourist destination.
machu-picchu.name: Machu Picchu

llaqtapata.story: As a traveller, you can come to Llaqtapata—pronounced “yakta-pahta”—an archaeological site about 5 km west of Machu Picchu, high on a ridge between the Ahobamba and Santa Teresa drainages. Hiram Bingham first discovered it in 1912 and found evidence that some Inca chieftain had built his home here, with ten or a dozen buildings in the plan. The Thomson and Ziegler expedition of 2003 concluded that its location along the Inca Trail suggested it was an important rest stop and roadside shrine on the journey to Machu Picchu. It was connected with Machu Picchu by a continuation of the Inca Trail leading onward into the Vilcabamba, and it probably played an important astronomical function during the solstices and equinoxes.
llaqtapata.name: Llaqtapata

patallacta.story: As you travel toward Machu Picchu, you can find Patallacta southeast of the site, at the confluence of the Cusichaca and Vilcanota rivers on a mountain named Patallacta, in Peru’s Cusco Region, Urubamba Province, Machupicchu District. On his way to Machu Picchu, Hiram Bingham passed Patallacta—sometimes called Llaqtapata, as shown by a sign at a check-point along the Inca Trail—and his associate Herman Tucker reported that the town contained about one hundred houses, with important sites including Huayllabamba above it and the start of the Classic Inca Trail 1.5 km away. This site housed many occupants, including travellers and soldiers who manned the nearby hill fort of Willkaraqay, and a shrine with rounded walls known as Pulpituyuq that had religious and ceremonial functions. Manco Inca Yupanqui burned Patallacta in 1536, destroying settlements along the Inca road system during his retreat from Cusco to discourage Spanish pursuit, so the Spanish never discovered the Inca Trail to Machu Picchu or any of its settlements.
patallacta.name: Patallacta

runkuraqay.story: Traveller, Runkuraqay is an archaeological site on a mountain of the same name in Peru, in the Cusco Region, Urubamba Province, Machupicchu District. Its name comes from Quechua: runku, basket, and raqay, shed, derelict house, or ruin. The ruins lie on the southern slope of the mountain Runkuraqay near the Runkuraqay pass, southeast of the archaeological site Machu Picchu, south of the Vilcanota river, northeast of the archaeological site Sayacmarca, and southeast of the site Qunchamarka. Hiram Bingham III visited the site in April 1915, and Paul Fejos visited in 1940.
runkuraqay.name: Runkuraqay

puyupatamarca.story: Traveller, along the Inca Trail in the Urubamba Valley of Peru, you can visit Puyupatamarca, also called Phuyupatamarca. At roughly 3600 meters, this archaeological site is known as "La Ciudad entre la Niebla," or "The City Above the Clouds." Its Inca ruins include five small stone baths. During the wet season, those baths contain constant fresh running water.
puyupatamarca.name: Puyupatamarca

tunquiorjo.story: As you travel through the Andes of Peru, Tunquiorjo is a mountain about 4,200 m high. Its name possibly comes from Quechua tunki, the Andean cock-of-the-rock, and urqu, mountain—“Andean cock-of-the-rock mountain.” You can place it in the Cusco Region, La Convención Province, Huayopata District, and Urubamba Province, Machupicchu District, in the northwestern extensions of the Urubamba mountain range. It lies northeast of the archaeological site of Machu Picchu.
tunquiorjo.name: Tunquiorjo

paljay.story: Take a moment to think of Paljay, also known as Palcay, a 5,422 metres (17,789 ft) mountain in the Vilcabamba Range. It is located in the Andes of Peru, in the region of Cusco. May that high mountain in the Vilcabamba Range, in the Andes of Peru, in the region of Cusco, be a warm presence on your journey.
paljay.name: Paljay

curcurorjo.story: Traveller, as you travel, let Curcurorjo stay with you. It is a mountain in the Andes of Peru, about 4,400 m high, in the Cusco Region, La Convención Province, Huayopata District, and in the Urubamba Province, Machupicchu District. Curcurorjo lies in the northwestern extensions of the Urubamba mountain range, northeast of the archaeological site of Machu Picchu. Its name possibly comes from Quechua k'urkur, Chusquea scandens, and urqu, mountain, meaning "k'urkur mountain."
curcurorjo.name: Curcurorjo
